stem: Which formula gives the **mark-up**?

options.rationale: Correct: mark-up is calculated on cost.
This is the gross profit margin.
This is the profit margin (net profit percentage).
This shows cost as a share of sales, not mark-up.

explanation: Mark-up = gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100; margin uses revenue as the denominator.

stem: Revenue was US\$64,000 and gross profit was US\$19,200. What was the gross profit margin?

options.rationale: This is the mark-up: gross profit has been divided by cost of sales.
This is cost of sales as a percentage of revenue.
Revenue has been divided by gross profit, the formula upside down.

stem: Cost of sales was US\$45,000 and gross profit was US\$15,300. What was the mark-up?

options.rationale: This is the margin: gross profit has been divided by revenue.
This is 100% minus the mark-up, which has no meaning here.
This is cost of sales as a percentage of revenue.

stem: A business had sales of US\$88,000, sales returns of US\$3,000 and a profit for the year of US\$10,200. What was the profit margin (net profit percentage)?

options.rationale: Sales returns have not been deducted from revenue.
Sales returns have been added to revenue instead of deducted.
This is 100% minus the profit margin.

stem: A company has issued shares of US\$150,000, reserves of US\$42,000 and a long-term loan of US\$48,000. Profit for the year after loan interest of US\$3,600 was US\$26,400. What is the return on capital employed?

options.rationale: Profit after interest has been used; interest must be added back.
The loan has been left out of capital employed.
Only issued shares have been used; reserves and the loan are part of capital employed.

explanation: Profit before interest = 26,400 + 3,600 = 30,000. Capital employed = 240,000. ROCE = 12.5%.
hints: Capital employed = issued shares + reserves + non-current liabilities.

stem: A trader's gross profit margin stayed the same but her profit margin fell. What is the most likely reason?

options.rationale: Higher buying prices would reduce the gross profit margin too.
Lower selling prices would reduce the gross profit margin.
Theft raises cost of sales and lowers the gross profit margin.

options.content: Her expenses rose faster than her sales
options.rationale: Correct: only items below gross profit have changed.

explanation: With a steady gross margin, the fall must come from expenses (or lower other income).

stem: Which change would **increase** a shop's gross profit margin, all else being equal?

options.content: Paying the shop assistant a higher wage
options.rationale: Wages are an expense below gross profit.

options.content: Buying goods in bulk at a lower unit cost
options.rationale: Correct: lower cost of sales for the same revenue raises gross profit.

options.content: Giving customers a larger discount on selling prices
options.rationale: Lower selling prices reduce the margin.
Advertising is an expense below gross profit.

explanation: Gross profit margin depends only on selling prices and the cost of goods sold.
hints: Only revenue and cost of sales affect gross profit.

stem: In the Cambridge formula for ROCE, capital employed is …

options.content: total assets less all non-current liabilities
options.rationale: This is equity, which leaves out the loans.

options.content: current assets less current liabilities at the year end
options.rationale: This is working capital.
Correct: the long-term finance of the company.

options.content: issued shares plus reserves plus current liabilities
options.rationale: Current liabilities are short-term finance, not capital employed.

explanation: The syllabus prints capital employed as issued shares + reserves + non-current liabilities.

stem: For any business making a gross profit, the mark-up is always a higher percentage than the gross profit margin.
explanation: True. Both use the same gross profit, but cost of sales is smaller than revenue, so dividing by it gives a larger percentage.

stem: Rent received by a trader is included in revenue when calculating the gross profit margin.
explanation: False. Revenue is sales of goods (net of returns). Rent received is other income, added after gross profit.

stem: In ZIMSEC questions, the net profit percentage is net profit divided by sales, multiplied by 100.
explanation: True. It is the same ratio Cambridge calls the profit margin.

stem: Match each ratio with the figure it is divided by.
explanation: Margin and profit margin divide by revenue; mark-up by cost of sales; ROCE by capital employed. Average inventory is used for inventory turnover.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: A margin of 30% means that every US\$100 of sales gives US\$ {{blank:a}} of gross profit and has a cost of sales of US\$ {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Margin is a percentage of selling price: 30 of every 100 is gross profit, 70 is cost.

stem: Sales US\$146,500; sales returns US\$2,300; gross profit US\$41,860. Calculate the gross profit margin, to one decimal place.
Thandeka's revenue was US\$78,400 and her cost of sales US\$53,900. Calculate her mark-up, to one decimal place.
explanation: Gross profit = 78,400 − 53,900 = 24,500. Mark-up = 24,500 ÷ 53,900 × 100 = 45.5%. Dividing by revenue gives the margin, 31.3%.
workedSolution: 1. Gross profit = 78,400 − 53,900 = 24,500. Mark-up = 24,500 ÷ 53,900 × 100 = 45.5%. Dividing by revenue gives the margin, 31.3%.

stem: Sipho is a sole trader. At 31 December 2025 his capital was US\$58,000 and he had a bank loan of US\$12,000 repayable in 2029. His profit for the year was US\$9,850 after loan interest of US\$960. Calculate his return on capital employed, to one decimal place.
explanation: Profit before interest = 9,850 + 960 = 10,810. Capital employed = 58,000 + 12,000 = 70,000. ROCE = 15.4%. Using profit after interest gives 14.1%; leaving out the loan gives 18.6%.
workedSolution: 1. Profit before interest = 9,850 + 960 = 10,810. Capital employed = 58,000 + 12,000 = 70,000. ROCE = 15.4%. Using profit after interest gives 14.1%; leaving out the loan gives 18.6%.
hints: For a sole trader, capital employed = owner's capital + non-current liabilities.
Add the interest back to profit.

stem: Rudo's gross profit margin fell from 35.0% to 31.0%. Suggest **two** reasons for the fall.

points.description: Cost prices rose and were not passed on to customers
Selling prices were reduced / more discounts / theft or damage of inventory / change to lower-margin goods

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Her suppliers may have raised prices without her raising her own, or she cut her selling prices to attract customers.

explanation: The gross margin depends only on buying and selling prices and inventory losses.
hints: Think only about revenue and cost of sales.

stem: A sole trader's ROCE is 4.5%. A bank fixed deposit pays 7%. Advise the owner what this comparison suggests.

points.description: The business earns less than a risk-free deposit would
So the owner should improve profitability or consider whether the capital would be better invested elsewhere (allowing for non-financial reasons)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Her money earns only 4.5% in the business, less than the 7% it could earn safely in the bank. She should look for ways to raise profit, or consider whether the business is worth the risk.

explanation: ROCE is compared with the return on alternative, lower-risk investments.
hints: Compare the return with what the money could earn elsewhere at lower risk.

parts.stem: Explain the difference between what the gross profit margin and the profit margin show.

points.description: Gross profit margin shows profit from buying and selling (prices and cost of goods) per dollar of sales
Profit margin shows what is left per dollar of sales after all expenses (and other income), so it reflects control of expenses

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The gross margin shows how much of each dollar of sales is left after the cost of the goods, so it reflects pricing and buying. The profit margin shows what remains after all running expenses, so it also reflects how well expenses are controlled.

stem:
Chinhoyi Feeds Ltd extended its warehouse in 2025, financed by an additional loan. Extracts from its financial statements:

|  | 2024 US\$ | 2025 US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 210,000 | 248,000 |
| Gross profit | 67,200 | 74,400 |
| Profit for the year | 23,100 | 22,320 |
| Loan interest (included in expenses) | 2,400 | 4,800 |
| Issued ordinary shares | 120,000 | 120,000 |
| Reserves | 38,000 | 51,000 |
| Non-current liabilities: loan | 30,000 | 60,000 |

In 2024 the gross profit margin was 32.0%, the profit margin 11.0% and the ROCE 13.6%.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the gross profit margin for 2025, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit margin for 2025, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the return on capital employed for 2025, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Profit before interest 22,320 + 4,800 = 27,120; capital employed 120,000 + 51,000 + 60,000 = 231,000; ROCE 11.7%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Profit before interest 22,320 + 4,800 = 27,120; capital employed 120,000 + 51,000 + 60,000 = 231,000; ROCE 11.7%.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Comment on the changes in the three ratios between 2024 and 2025 and evaluate whether the warehouse extension has been worthwhile so far.

points.description: Gross margin fell (32.0% to 30.0%): lower selling prices or higher costs
Profit margin fell (11.0% to 9.0%): expenses including the doubled interest grew faster than sales
ROCE fell (13.6% to 11.7%): the extra capital has not yet earned a matching return
Evaluation: revenue grew 18.1%, so the extension may pay off later; so far it has not been worthwhile on these figures

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: All three ratios fell. The gross margin dropped from 32.0% to 30.0%, suggesting cheaper selling prices or higher feed costs. The profit margin fell from 11.0% to 9.0% because expenses, including twice as much interest, rose faster than sales. ROCE fell from 13.6% to 11.7% because capital employed rose by US\$43,000 while profit before interest rose by only US\$1,620. Revenue grew by 18.1%, so the warehouse may pay off as sales grow, but so far it has reduced profitability.
